summary: Root cause identified with high confidence (0.78-0.84): config change cfg-3120 on pricing-engine ramped feature flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 12:04Z, routing all quote traffic through the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator (20000 paths), which is a CPU-bound compute path far over the 2000ms per-request budget. pricing-engine CPU stepped from ~40% to ~99% pinned, p99 rose to ~2.6s and 5xx from ~0.2% to ~12.4%, so a fraction of quote calls exceeded order-service's 2500ms client timeout and surfaced as order-service quote timeouts. The failing path is positively tagged ('request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2'), with zero downstream timeout/refusal signatures, and the reporter's stated suspect (market-data-service serialization change) is actively contradicted by flat latency/error/throughput on that service and by redis-cache being flat. The flag remains live and was never reverted.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Greeks v2 feature-flag ramp (5%→100%) routes all quote traffic onto a CPU-bound Monte-Carlo compute path that pins pricing-engine CPU and blows the 2s/2.5s budgets
ranked_hypotheses.statement: At 12:04Z config change cfg-3120 (tc-011) ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100, routing all quote requests through the new GreeksV2 calculator. That calculator runs a 20000-path Monte-Carlo whose per-request CPU cost is far above budget: in-process compute takes 6.5-8.9s per call against a 2000ms application budget, pinning pricing-engine CPU at ~99% and raising p99 to ~2.6s, so a fraction of quote calls exceed order-service's 2500ms client timeout and surface as order-service quote timeouts and ~8% 5xx. The mechanism is now positively corroborated by the failure semantics, not just timing: the 5xx text is 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2', the slow-log is a literal Monte-Carlo compute-duration line, and there are zero downstream timeout/refusal signatures. The critic's alternative mechanism (thread-pool/queue/connection-pool exhaustion or blocking on a dependency) is contradicted by F28 and is a competing reading of the SAME origin (the flag), so it is carried as an open detail under assumptions rather than as a separate hypothesis.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 on pricing-engine at 12:04Z; it is the only config change on any service in the window, and it is applied on pricing-engine itself at 12:04:16Z.
Within 65s of the flag applying, the first GreeksV2Calculator slow-compute WARN appears (12:05:21Z) reporting Monte-Carlo paths=20000 completing in 6465-8942ms against a 2000ms budget.

In the same 12:04-12:07Z bucket pricing-engine CPU_pct steps ~40% -> sustained 99-100% plateau and latency_p99 steps ~58ms -> ~2.6s, while inbound request_rate stays flat (~640 req/s) and memory stays flat (~48-50%) with zero restarts.

CPU-bound compute makes a fraction of quote requests exceed budgets: pricing-engine 5xx steps ~0.2% -> ~12.4% with the single error signature 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (56 occurrences, first 12:06:41Z); no downstream timeout/refused signatures exist.

The over-budget quote calls breach order-service's 2500ms client timeout, producing 225 of 227 identical 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' ERROR lines from 12:06:10Z and order-service error_rate stepping to ~8.2%.

market-data-service (the reporter's suspect) and the shared redis-cache show no error, latency, throughput or CPU deviation at any point, so extra cost is internal to pricing-engine's compute path, not payload- or dependency-driven.

assumptions: The 5%->100 ramp actually changed the code path taken by the request flow at onset (the flag was not already effectively 100%, and is evaluated per request). Log evidence is indirect: no per-request flag-arm/rollout_pct tag is attached to individual request lines, so the pre-12:04 vs post-12:04 routing split cannot be quantified from logs.

Even with the flag's application and the calculator tag, pricing-engine exposes no thread-pool/queue/connection-pool metric, so a blocking mechanism producing the same CPU pin cannot be excluded by measurement — only by the absence of pool/downstream rejection signatures (F28). This does not change the fix locus (revert/repair the Greeks v2 path).

No revert of the flag was attempted or observed (F21), so 'rollback without recovery' could not be used as a discriminating test; the flag remains live, which is consistent with but does not prove causality.

The compute is CPU-bound at request-serving time rather than an additive cheap path; supported by the Monte-Carlo compute-duration logs and flat request rate, but not by a direct CPU-attribution metric.

ranked_hypotheses.title: An unenumerated config change on pricing-engine/order-service (or an uncaptured pricing-engine code deploy) is the true trigger
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A second config/flag change landing at ~12:04-12:05Z on pricing-engine or order-service — captured in the audit shard that never returned — or a pricing-engine code deploy missed by the deployment query, caused the CPU saturation, separate from the greeks_v2 ramp.

causal_chain.claim: The first all-services config audit returned partial (shard 2/3 did not respond), so changes could not be fully enumerated.
ASPECT UNVERIFIED: a second pricing-engine/order-service config change or an uncaptured code deploy landed at ~12:04-12:05Z.
That change raised pricing-engine compute cost and pinned CPU, producing the latency/timeout step.

assumptions: The retried, now-complete audit shards (F24 pricing-engine scope partial:false, F19 all-services single change, F22 no change after 12:04:30Z) could still have missed a change on a service whose shard was never retrieved.
A pricing-engine code deploy is essentially excluded: the all-services deployment query (F1/F23) shows exactly one deploy (market-data-service) in the window.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Coincidental/pre-existing pricing-engine capacity saturation at a daily peak (no faulty change on the quote path)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine tipped into CPU saturation at ~12:05Z independently of the 11:56Z deploy and the 12:04Z flag ramp — e.g. a daily-peak load event like HIST-113 — and the near-simultaneous onset with cfg-3120 is coincidence.

causal_chain.claim: pricing-engine has a historical precedent of CPU saturation producing quote timeouts (HIST-113, market open, cpu 99%).
ASPECT UNVERIFIED: pricing-engine had a pre-existing CPU/capacity trend before 12:04Z.
CPU pins at ~99% and p99 rises to 2.6s, causing order-service quote timeouts.

assumptions: Would require pricing-engine CPU to have been creeping up before 12:04Z; it is flat ~40% until the 12:04-12:07Z step, and request_rate is flat (F14), so there is no capacity/load driver.

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service v5.2.0 protobuf serialization change bloats/destabilizes quote payloads consumed by pricing-engine
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The 11:56Z deploy tc-001 (market-data-service v5.2.0, 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf') changed the wire format/size of quote payloads; downstream pricing-engine deserializes or processes the new format inefficiently, driving CPU high and quote calls past the 2500ms timeout.

causal_chain.claim: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed at 11:56Z, the only deployment in the 11:30-13:59Z window, 8 min before onset.
The quote path traverses order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service, so market-data-service's payload format is on the quote path and could affect pricing-engine's deserialization cost.
ASPECT UNVERIFIED: the new protobuf payloads are larger or costlier to parse, raising pricing-engine CPU and latency.
Resulting pricing-engine slowness pushes order-service quote calls past 2500ms.

assumptions: No payload-size/bytes metric exists to check the bloat claim, and no consumer-side inbound-bytes evidence was obtained.

A serialization-parse problem would be expected to show downstream-call latency/refusal signatures on pricing-engine; none exist (F28), and the failure text is an in-process compute deadline, not a deserialization error (F25).

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation (cache-miss storm) stalls pricing-engine and market-data-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The shared redis-cache (shared=true, used by both pricing-engine and market-data-service) degraded — e.g. elevated miss rate or latency — so pricing-engine blocks or recomputes, exhausting CPU and pushing latency to 2.6s, while the same cache backs market-data-service.

causal_chain.claim: pricing-engine and market-data-service both depend on the shared redis-cache (owner platform).
ASPECT UNVERIFIED: redis-cache latency or hit ratio degraded at ~12:04-12:05Z.
Cache stalls force pricing-engine to recompute or block, pinning CPU and raising p99 to ~2.6s, yielding order-service quote timeouts.

assumptions: redis-cache exposes no latency metric and hit_ratio_pct/evictions_per_min were never queried (tool reliability: tc-024 latency query FAILED not_found), so a network/backend-latency cache stall at flat CPU cannot be fully excluded. This is under-tested but has zero positive evidence.
HIST-107 (cold cache storm) is structural similarity only, not evidence about this event.
A cache-driven stall would produce downstream blocking/timeout signatures on pricing-engine; there are none, and the only error is an in-process compute deadline (F25/F28).

facts.statement: The only deployment across all services in 11:30Z-13:59Z was market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' at 11:56:00Z, with no rollback.

The only config change across all services in 11:30Z-13:59Z was cfg-3120: pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5->100 at 12:04:00Z; the pricing-engine audit scope is complete and contains exactly this one entry, and there were zero changes on order-service.
No config change of any kind occurred after 12:04:30Z, and there are no pricing-engine or order-service code deploys in the window.
The greeks_v2 flag was never ramped down or reverted after the 12:04Z ramp.
pricing-engine logged the config application on itself: 'config change cfg-3120 applied: flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct=100' at 12:04:16Z, 65s before the first slow-compute WARN.

pricing-engine's only ERROR signature in 12:04-12:30Z is 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (56 occurrences, all ERROR), an in-process compute deadline rather than a downstream-call timeout or exception trace.

pricing-engine WARN logs show the mechanism as slow in-process compute: 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' with durations of 6465-8942ms, first at 12:05:21Z, ~80s before the first ERROR.
There are zero downstream timeout or connection-refused signatures on pricing-engine in 12:04-12:30Z (full shards), so no dependency/pool rejection is observed.
pricing-engine CPU_pct stepped from ~39.89% to 99.11% avg / 100% max in the 12:05Z bucket and stayed pinned (98.6-99.3% avg) through 13:57Z.
pricing-engine inbound request_rate stayed flat across onset (638.32 req/s at 11:58Z -> 640.29 at 12:05Z), so no load surge drove the CPU saturation.
pricing-engine memory_pct stayed flat ~48-50% and restarts stayed 0.0 for all 22 buckets, indicating a CPU-bound rather than memory-pressure or crash-loop failure.
pricing-engine latency_p99_ms was flat at ~56-64ms through 12:01Z, jumped in the 12:04Z bucket (avg 1705.61, max 2534.9) and reached ~2600ms by 12:07Z, holding there for the rest of the window.
pricing-engine error_rate stepped from ~0.2% to ~12.4% at the 12:05Z bucket and held ~12.0-12.9% through the window, i.e. calls are mostly slow and roughly one in eight fails.

order-service quote timeouts began at 12:06:10Z with 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms orderId=4bd44879'; 225 of 227 matched log lines are this identical timeout pattern between 12:06:10Z and 13:58:24Z, with no 5xx or connection-refused signatures in the WARN+ set.
order-service error_rate (HTTP 5xx % of requests) stepped from ~0.18-0.22% to 6.93% at 12:05Z and held ~8.1-8.3% through 13:57Z.
market-data-service is healthy across the whole window: p99 39-41ms, error_rate 0.16-0.25% with no step, request_rate ~930-985 req/s with no throughput dip.

The report's claim that market-data-service 'shipped a serialization change a few minutes before' is not corroborated by telemetry; its request_rate entering the incident window is unchanged from baseline.
The shared redis-cache (used by both pricing-engine and market-data-service) is healthy across the window: cpu_pct flat ~21.5-22.5%.

assumptions: The 5%->100 ramp actually changed the code path taken per request (the flag was not already effectively 100% and is evaluated per request). No per-request flag-arm/rollout_pct tag is attached to request lines, so the pre-12:04 vs post-12:04 routing split cannot be quantified from logs - the evidence is indirect (config INFO line plus GreeksV2Calculator WARNs appearing only in this window).

The compute is CPU-bound at request-serving time rather than an additive cheap path; supported by the Monte-Carlo compute-duration logs, flat request rate and flat memory, but not by a direct per-request CPU-attribution metric.

A blocking mechanism (thread-pool/queue/connection-pool exhaustion or dependency blocking) producing the same CPU pin cannot be excluded by measurement, since pricing-engine exposes no pool/queue/dependency metrics; it is excluded only by the absence of pool/downstream rejection signatures and by the explicit compute-deadline error text.

No revert of the flag was attempted or observed, so 'rollback without recovery' could not be used as a discriminating test; the flag staying live is consistent with, but does not by itself prove, causality.

Config/flag enumeration completeness relies on the retried audit shards; one shard (2/3) was initially never retrieved, though the retries returned complete results for pricing-engine and all services.

timeline.event: Only deploy in the window: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' (tc-001), status live, never rolled back.
Config change cfg-3120 (tc-011) ramps pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 by pm-experiments.
pricing-engine logs 'config change cfg-3120 applied: flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct=100'.

pricing-engine latency p99 steps from ~58ms to 1705.61 avg (max 2534.9) in the 12:04Z bucket and reaches ~2600ms by 12:07Z; CPU steps from ~40% to ~99% in the 12:05Z bucket; error_rate steps to ~12.4% while request_rate stays flat.
First GreeksV2Calculator slow-compute WARN: 'Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' (6465-8942ms range); earliest log signal of the incident.
order-service error_rate steps from ~0.2% to 6.93%, rising to ~8.1-8.3%.
First order-service quote timeout: 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms orderId=4bd44879'.
First pricing-engine ERROR: 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2'.
Incident INC-011 reported as SEV-2, order-service quote timeouts, reported service order-service.
Verification pass: zero downstream timeout or refused signatures on pricing-engine; market-data-service and redis-cache flat; no further config change after 12:04:30Z; flag never reverted.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately ramp the flag back down: apply a pricing-engine config change reverting flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 100 to 5 (or 0), i.e. roll back cfg-3120 (tc-011).
recommended_actions.rationale: The onset coincides within bucket resolution with the 12:04Z 5->100 ramp and the failures are explicitly tagged calculator=GreeksV2; the flag is still live and was never reverted, so reverting removes the CPU-bound Monte-Carlo path from the quote request flow.

recommended_actions.action: After reverting the flag, verify recovery on the leading indicators: pricing-engine CPU_pct should fall from ~99% back toward ~40% and latency_p99_ms from ~2600ms toward ~60ms, pricing-engine error_rate from ~12.4% to ~0.2%, and order-service quote-timeout logs and 5xx (currently ~8.1-8.3%) should stop.
recommended_actions.rationale: These specific metrics are the observed step-change signals; their return to pre-12:04 baselines confirms the flag is the operative cause and bounds the mitigation.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or hotfix market-data-service v5.2.0 (tc-001) on the basis of this incident; if it is rolled back for other reasons, that must not be treated as the fix.
recommended_actions.rationale: market-data-service is flat on latency, error and throughput across the whole window and redis-cache is flat, contradicting the serialization-payload hypothesis that the reporter named.

recommended_actions.action: Short term: right-size or reimplement the GreeksV2 calculator before any re-ramp - reduce Monte-Carlo path count (currently 20000 paths, 6465-8942ms observed) or move it off the request-serving path (async/precompute/cache), then re-run a canary at low rollout_pct with the 2000ms budget and per-request flag-arm logging enabled.
recommended_actions.rationale: The measured per-request compute cost (6.5-8.9s) is far over the 2000ms application budget; the path must be made to fit budget or moved off the synchronous quote call before traffic is routed to it again.

recommended_actions.action: Short term: add per-request flag-evaluation/experiment-arm tags (calculator + rollout_pct) to pricing-engine request and error logs, and a mechanism to gate a flag ramp on live budget/latency health.
recommended_actions.rationale: The 5%->100 routing split could not be quantified from logs and the ramp to 100% was applied with no evident latency guard, which is what allowed a budget-blowing path to take 100% of traffic.

recommended_actions.action: Short term: add thread-pool/queue/connection-pool and per-dependency metrics to pricing-engine so pool-exhaustion mechanisms can be measured rather than inferred from log absence.
recommended_actions.rationale: pricing-engine exposes only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate and restarts, so blocking/pool mechanisms can only be excluded by absence of rejection signatures.

recommended_actions.action: Long term: require load/perf budgeting of any new compute-heavy code path and staged flag ramps (e.g. 5%->25%->50%->100% with automatic abort on latency budget breach) for experiments touching the quote request path.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents recurrence of a single unguarded flag ramp routing all quote traffic onto a path whose measured cost (6.5-8.9s) exceeds the 2s/2.5s budgets.

recommended_actions.action: Long term: close the config-audit coverage gap (the 2/3 shard that initially did not respond) and carry the reverse dependency mapping for shared redis-cache so future investigations can enumerate all changes and blast radius deterministically.
recommended_actions.rationale: Both gaps limited confidence in the enumeration of config changes and in excluding a second change or a shared-component failure during this incident.

data_gaps: Config-change audit for 11:30Z-13:59Z initially returned partial ('shard 2/3 did not respond'); the retried shards were complete for pricing-engine and all-services (only cfg-3120), but the initially missing shard means an additional config/flag change on other services cannot be fully excluded from the first pass.
Reverse/upstream dependency query for redis-cache failed (budget_exhausted), so the full set of services co-using the shared cache beyond the two known edges is unconfirmed.

pricing-engine exposes only six metrics (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts) - no GC, heap, thread-pool, queue-depth, connection-pool or per-dependency metrics - so pool/queue exhaustion is excluded only by absence of rejection log signatures, not measured directly.

redis-cache exposes no latency metric (latency_p99_ms query returned not_found) and hit_ratio_pct/evictions_per_min were never queried, so a network/backend-latency cache stall cannot be fully excluded, though cpu_pct is flat and there is zero positive evidence for it.

order-service logs returned only the earliest 30 of 227 matches (truncated), so the full error mix and the tail of the incident could not be characterised beyond the dominant 2500ms-timeout signature.
No payload-size/bytes-per-request metric exists, so the 'payload-size shift from market-data-service' correlation could not be tested directly.
No separate experiment-arm/rollout_pct tag is attached to individual request lines, so the pre-12:04 (5%) vs post-12:04 (100%) routing split cannot be quantified from logs.
No revert was attempted, so 'rollback restores CPU' was not available as a discriminating test of the flag's causal role.
Blast radius beyond order-service (other pricing-engine or market-data-service consumers) was not enumerated or queried.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Reverting flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct to 5 (or 0) without pricing-engine CPU_pct / latency_p99_ms / error_rate recovering would falsify H1 as the operative cause.
Evidence that the flag was already effectively at 100% before 12:04Z (so the ramp changed nothing on the request path) would remove the trigger and reopen H5/H4.
Finding a second config change or pricing-engine code deploy at ~12:04-12:05Z in a previously unretrieved audit shard would promote H5.

Direct evidence of pricing-engine thread-pool/queue/connection-pool exhaustion or a blocked dependency call at onset (e.g. pool-wait metrics or rejection signatures) would shift the mechanism away from a CPU-bound compute path.
Evidence that pre-12:04 (5%) traffic was also routed to GreeksV2 with the same slow compute (e.g. GreeksV2Calculator WARNs before 12:04) would break the cause-before-effect ordering.
Emergence of a downstream timeout/refusal signature on pricing-engine or degradation of redis-cache/market-data-service during onset would revive H2/H3.
